title: Encoded Polyline Encoder: Coordinates to String
description: Encode coordinate sequences into Google's polyline format with the Encoded Polyline Encoder — precision-5 strings for APIs and URLs. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, two points — Times Square (40.7580, −73.9855) to JFK (40.6413, −73.7781) — encode to the compact string opwwFjhqbMjxUgog@, ready to ride in a URL or an API call.
quick_answer: The Encoded Polyline Encoder compresses a sequence of latitude/longitude points into an encoded polyline string — the compact format routing APIs use to carry routes. Enter the points and read the string: coordinates scaled, delta-encoded and chunked into printable characters, exactly as Google’s published algorithm specifies.

body.t: Static map images and route previews take paths as encoded polylines. Encode here instead of pasting fragile coordinate lists into URLs. Verify any string with the
A 500-point route as text coordinates is a paragraph; as a polyline, a line. Databases and config files appreciate the diet.
OSRM, GraphHopper and Google-shaped APIs accept polylines as geometry input. Encoding locally makes requests self-contained.
Delta encoding on real routes shows why the format works: consecutive points differ by little, so their differences compress to a character or two.

Encode (38.5, −120.2), (40.7, −120.95), (43.252, −126.453) and the algorithm must return _p~iF~ps|U_ulLnnqC_mqNvxq`@ — Google’s documented example. An encoder that reproduces the canonical string implements the standard; anything else implements a rumour.

A highway route’s points step ~0.01° at a time — deltas near 1,000 in scaled units, two characters each. The absolute coordinates would cost five or six. The string’s brevity is the road’s smoothness, measured.

popular_table.title: The encoding, step by step
rows: Multiply latitude and longitude by 100,000; round to integers
Take differences from the previous point (first point from 0,0)
Split into 5-bit chunks, add 63, emit as ASCII
popular_table.note: Output characters fall in ASCII 63 (‘?’) to 126 (‘~’) — URL-hostile characters like the backslash do not occur, but ‘@’, ‘`’ and ‘|’ do, so URL-embedding still wants percent-encoding.

faq: Five decimal places — the standard. Points are rounded to the format’s grain (~1.1 m); finer source precision is respectfully discarded, which matters for survey tracks.
Latitude,longitude per point — the format’s own order, opposite to GeoJSON’s. The encoder takes pairs as the tool presents them; swapping produces a mirrored route in the southern ocean.
Can it encode a single point?
Yes — a one-point polyline is legal and decodes to that point. Lines are the day job, but the format does not insist.
Some ecosystems (certain Mapbox/OSRM configurations) speak precision 6. This encoder writes the canonical 5; know your consumer before shipping strings across dialects.
Thousands encode instantly. URL length limits (~2,000 characters in conservative stacks) cap practical web use — long routes get simplified first, a separate and honest craft.
Only the sub-grain rounding (under ~1.1 m). The delta chain itself is exact — decode your string and diff the points when trust is low.
Not in the standard format. Altitude-carrying dialects exist (flex polylines); standard consumers would read your altitudes as geography and wander.
